lead.headline: Academy of Motion Picture Arts to give 15 statuettes at a dinner tonight
lead.deck: About 270 guests at five dollars a plate at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel; the pictures honoured are silent, as pictures are; the awards to be read in fifteen minutes
lead.body: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences will give 15 gold statuettes for pictures shown in 1927 and 1928 at a dinner at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel at 8 p.m. tonight, Pacific time, its secretary states. About 270 guests have paid five dollars a plate. Mr. Douglas Fairbanks will preside. The awards are to be read in about fifteen minutes. The hotel's house system will record the dinner, and the Academy will send the record east by wire at 1 a.m.

columns.headline: Fire and gas in the Cleveland Clinic's film store; at least 107 dead
columns.body: Fire and gas from the basement film store of the Cleveland Clinic filled the building at about 11:30 a.m. yesterday, the wire states, and at least 107 persons had died by midnight. The Clinic's house system recorded the alarm at 11:31 a.m.

columns.headline: Process server tries the Signal Ground Rents post box a fourth time
columns.body: Mr. Raab, process server, tried the post office box of Signal Ground Rents Inc. a fourth time yesterday and found it 'not rented.' The man in the grey coat who examined the nine May receipts at the court clerk's on Tuesday has not been seen since.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin to leave Friedrichshafen for Lakehurst this morning
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin will leave Friedrichshafen for Lakehurst this morning with passengers and mail, Dr. Hugo Eckener commanding, the Berlin wire states. The Navy's station at Lakehurst will listen for her from noon tomorrow. On her last crossing, in October, she was heard over Long Island before she was seen.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the eighth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 70. Thursday. Hollywood dines tonight. The pictures will not be speaking.

lead.headline: Hollywood dines its silent partners, and the pictures take no calls
lead.deck: Two hundred and seventy swells pay five dollars a plate to hand gold dolls to pictures that cannot thank them; the dinner will talk, and the guests of honour will flicker
lead.body: Tonight in Hollywood two hundred and seventy people will eat chicken at five dollars a plate and give fifteen gold statuettes to motion pictures, which cannot attend, being on a reel. A picture, for those who have not paid to see one, is a talker without the talk: a grey room on a wall where people move their mouths and an organist guesses. It costs a family a week's milk. Mr. Fairbanks presides. The hotel will record every word, and the guests of honour will say none.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Must I dress to see a picture?'
columns.body: Madam, at the Paramount, yes, and at a dollar a seat you will want your money's worth. The picture will not hear you. You may cough, whisper and unwrap a toffee. The operator went once, in 1927, and says it was like a long telephone call with the sound off.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Eight nights since the sermon, and the band's gone quiet again
columns.body: WORS has not been heard since Dr. Hartwell asked his question on the seventh. Our office boy has left pin ninety-seven in the map, at the river, and dusts it. Mr. Pike's night clerk says 'No' again, and seems relieved to be saying it.

columns.headline: Raab rings the box again, and Signal Ground Rents leaves him on hold
columns.body: Mr. Raab tried Signal Ground Rents' post box a fourth time. Not rented. Meanwhile the grey coat who read the nine receipts at the court clerk's and said 'Correct' has gone back to wherever grey coats go when nobody is asking for May.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Cleveland counts more than a hundred dead at the Clinic. No jokes again tonight.

lead.headline: 'Wings' named the year's outstanding picture at the Academy's first dinner
lead.deck: Fifteen statuettes given in fifteen minutes; Mr. Jannings, who has sailed for Germany, received his before leaving; a special award to Warner Brothers for a picture with speech in it
lead.body: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences named 'Wings,' a picture of fliers, the outstanding production of 1927 and 1928 at its dinner at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel last night. Miss Janet Gaynor and Mr. Emil Jannings were named for acting, Mr. Jannings having received his statuette before sailing for Germany. A special award went to Warner Brothers for 'The Jazz Singer,' in which the performers are heard. The record of the dinner, received by wire at 4:10 a.m., runs 22 minutes, chiefly applause.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin reported turning back over Spain with two engines stopped
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin, which left Friedrichshafen for Lakehurst yesterday, was reported turning back over the coast of Spain at 2 a.m. today with two of her five engines stopped, the Madrid wire states. Her wireless operator was heard at Bay Shore asking for French weather.

columns.headline: First charge under the Listening Act laid against an Elmhurst landlord
columns.body: Mr. Gideon Pruett, owner of a six-family house on Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, was summoned yesterday under section 14 of the Listening Act, in force since April 4, for selling a room's record without a licence, the District Attorney states. It is the first charge laid under the Act.

columns.headline: Paramount to show 'Wings' again from Monday; seats at one and two dollars
columns.body: The Paramount Theatre will show 'Wings' again from Monday at four performances daily, seats at one dollar and two dollars, the management states. The picture runs two hours and twenty minutes, with an orchestra. Patrons are asked not to speak to the picture, 'it being unable to reply.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Alphonse Capone of Chicago was arrested last night outside a Philadelphia picture theatre carrying a revolver, the wire states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 73. Friday. A gangster got a year. Wings got a statuette. Party Line got nothing.

lead.headline: Capone gets a year in sixteen hours, Philadelphia's fastest connection
lead.deck: Chicago's best-known businessman walks out of a picture house into two detectives, pleads guilty before lunch, and goes to Holmesburg with his bodyguard
lead.body: Mr. Alphonse Capone of Chicago went to the pictures in Philadelphia last night, came out at the end, and found two detectives waiting by the box office. He had a revolver. So did his bodyguard. This morning both pleaded guilty, and by lunch both had a year. Sixteen hours from the picture house to the prison wagon, which Philadelphia says is a record and which the court's own machine took down in forty seconds flat. Chicago is astonished.

columns.headline: Party Line holds for a seventh Friday, and the parcel window stays shut
columns.body: Seven Fridays. Party Line was in the parcel window at four, tail round her feet, and nothing came from Corona. Sergeant Moran says the lineman's warrant is still current. At six she went to the warm end of the board. The open window has lost interest.

columns.headline: Zeppelin loses two engines over Spain, and Lakehurst is left holding the mast
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin left Germany for Lakehurst yesterday and was over Spain by night with two engines stopped and her wireless asking for French weather. She came down this afternoon at a French naval field near Toulon. Lakehurst has its mast up and nothing to tie to it.

columns.headline: Wings takes off with the gold, and the talking picture gets a courtesy call
columns.body: Wings was named the picture of the year last night. Warner Brothers got a special statuette for The Jazz Singer, in which you hear the actors. Hollywood thought this enterprising. Queens, which hears its neighbours through two walls nightly, thought it ordinary. The organists said nothing, loudly.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Zeppelin is down safe at Cuers. Her passengers are going home by train, and hearing all about it.

lead.headline: Week's count: 1,520 night calls on the tone in Queens and 455 in Brooklyn
lead.deck: Brooklyn's calls from five districts, Park Slope reporting for the first time; the Brooklyn Courier declines to print the figures; Dr. Rastin's meter unchanged at 41 cycles
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,520 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,410 the week before, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The Brooklyn Exchange logged 455, Mr. Oswald Pryce states, from Greenpoint, Williamsburg, Bushwick, Flatbush and Park Slope, the last for the first time. The Brooklyn Courier states that it 'will not print figures it has no knowledge of.' Dr. Emil Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles. Queens Light & Power made no statement.

columns.headline: Mr. Capone pleads guilty at Philadelphia and is sentenced to a year
columns.body: Mr. Alphonse Capone of Chicago and his bodyguard, Mr. Frank Rio, arrested on Thursday evening outside a Philadelphia picture theatre carrying revolvers, pleaded guilty yesterday and were each sentenced to a year, the Philadelphia wire states. The court's record of the pleas runs 40 seconds.

columns.headline: Licences: 304 granted in the week, 1,061 in all; 2,890 forms returned
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 304 licences under the Listening Act in the five days to Friday, 1,061 in all, his office states. Of 6,000 forms delivered on April 9, 2,890 have been returned. Mr. Gideon Pruett of Elmhurst has not returned his.

columns.headline: No parcel for the Exchange's Position 43 on a seventh Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the seventh Friday without one, the supervisor states. Detective Sergeant Edward Moran states that the warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, 'remains current.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Kentucky Derby will be run at Churchill Downs this afternoon on a track reported 'heavy,' and carried by wire.

speaker.ear: Cloudy. High 67. Saturday. Brooklyn hears more and more of what it doesn't hear.

lead.headline: Park Slope picks up the Hum, and the Courier goes deaf on principle
lead.deck: Four hundred and fifty-five Brooklyn callers this week from five districts; Mr. Tully will print no figure he has no knowledge of, and has arranged to have none
lead.body: The Hum has reached Park Slope, which will be upset, Park Slope having always considered itself above that sort of thing. Four hundred and fifty-five Brooklyn callers this week rang their exchange between one and four in the morning to report the low tone, against fifteen hundred and twenty in Queens. The Brooklyn Courier says it will not print figures it has no knowledge of. Mr. Tully has a fine house in Park Slope. We rang it at two this morning. It was engaged.

columns.headline: Derby on a heavy track today, and every set in Kentucky turns up the volume
columns.body: The Kentucky Derby is run this afternoon at Churchill Downs in the mud, and the wire will carry it to every parlour in Queens with a set and a dollar on. Our tip is the smallest horse in the race. Our tipster is the smallest man in the office.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why is Position 43 so quiet on Fridays?'
columns.body: Sir, Position 43 is where Party Line sits. On Fridays at four she waits at the parcel window for a tin from Corona that has not come in seven weeks. The operators keep their voices down. It is not a rule. It is manners.

columns.headline: Capone's year: the Philadelphia court sets a speed record on the record
columns.body: Forty seconds, the court's own machine says, for Mr. Capone and Mr. Rio to plead guilty yesterday. A year each. Chicago is said to be listening to the record for clues. There are none. He said 'Guilty.' Philadelphia has had it framed.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Clyde Van Dusen, the smallest horse in the field, won the Derby in the mud. Our tipster is insufferable.

editorial.headline: Mother's Day at the Fenn garden party
editorial.body: Mr. Lucius Fenn, broker, philanthropist and, we are proud to say, proprietor of this newspaper, gave his annual Mother's Day garden party at Forest Hills on Sunday in aid of his Widows' and Orphans' Trust, which invests the savings of the borough's widows at a guaranteed nine percent. Among the guests, our society column reports, was a lady in a black wide-brimmed hat whom nobody could name, who danced twice with Mr. Fenn and asked to see the Trust's books. Mr. Fenn, who is a gentleman, showed her the garden instead. We mention this only to assure our proprietor that this newspaper stands behind him, behind the Trust and behind the garden. Especially the garden.

lead.headline: Little America sends a birthday message for a girl of nine in Sunnyside
lead.deck: Heard at Bay Shore at 10:12 p.m. from Commander Byrd's winter quarters; a dog driver's message to his daughter, read twice at his request; the camp 'all well, 52 below'
lead.body: The Navy's station at Bay Shore heard Commander Byrd's winter quarters at Little America at 10:12 p.m. yesterday, the camp reporting 'all well, 52 below.' At the request of Mr. Alton Fenwick, a dog driver, a message for his daughter in Sunnyside, nine today, was read twice: 'Happy birthday. It is dark here all day and I have saved you a piece of it. Tell your mother the dogs are fine.' The station relayed it by wire at 10:40 p.m.

columns.headline: Clyde Van Dusen wins the Kentucky Derby on a heavy track at Churchill Downs
columns.body: Clyde Van Dusen, a small gelding named for his trainer, won the Kentucky Derby at Churchill Downs yesterday on a heavy track, the Louisville wire states. The wire's record of the race has the crowd's noise rising for two minutes and ten seconds.

columns.headline: Flushing pastor repeats Dr. Hartwell's question over WLBQ at 11 p.m.
columns.body: The Rev. Amos Lyle of the Flushing Free Methodist Church closed a sermon over WLBQ at 11 p.m. Friday with 'Is anyone in this house listening?' WORS 1610 was not heard. The Exchange logged 92 calls. Dr. Hartwell stated that he 'did not suggest it.'

columns.headline: Mr. Dolan's listener logs 'a band, rain, nothing else' on the ninth day
columns.body: The log of Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan's 'office to hear the ground' at Steinway Street and Broadway for Friday reads 'a band, rain, nothing else,' his campaign states. Alderman John Feeney states that the office 'has heard everything except the Commission.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the eleventh night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 69. Sunday. Somebody at the bottom of the world is nine today. Not him. Her.

lead.headline: Long distance from Little America: a birthday girl gets a piece of the dark
lead.deck: Mr. Fenwick, dog driver, has the Navy read his message twice; Sunnyside hears it before midnight; the dogs are said to be fine
lead.body: A girl in Sunnyside is nine today, and last night at twelve minutes past ten the Navy at Bay Shore heard her father wish her many happy returns from Little America, where it is dark all day. Mr. Fenwick drives dogs for Commander Byrd. He asked for the message to be read twice. It said he had saved her a piece of the dark. The wire brought it to Sunnyside by eleven, on a record, and she has put the record under her pillow.

columns.headline: Smallest horse in the mud wins the Derby, and our tipster's call goes through
columns.body: Clyde Van Dusen, the smallest horse in the field, came home first at Louisville yesterday through mud to his knees. Our tipster, the smallest man in this office, had a dollar on him at long odds and has been ringing his mother since. She has asked him to stop.

columns.headline: Flushing preacher asks the same question, and gets dead air for his trouble
columns.body: The Rev. Mr. Lyle of Flushing ended his sermon on WLBQ on Friday with Dr. Hartwell's question, word for word. Ninety-two people rang the Exchange. WORS said nothing. Dr. Hartwell says he did not suggest it. Mr. Lyle says the question was not copyrighted.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a dinner in Hollywood, and every cough on the wire
columns.body: Darlings, the Academy's dinner record came east on the wire and the Listening Lady has played it four times. Twenty-two minutes. Applause, cutlery, Mr. Fairbanks, more applause. At eleven minutes somebody asks for the salt and is refused. One hopes it was a director.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Fenwick's girl is asleep with the record under her pillow. Good night, Little America.

lead.headline: Elmhurst landlord arraigned today in the first case under the Listening Act
lead.deck: Mr. Gideon Pruett charged with selling a tenant's kitchen record to a casualty adjuster for 15 dollars; his house system 'of a quality the State has not licensed before'
lead.body: Mr. Gideon Pruett, owner of a six-family house on Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, will be arraigned before Magistrate Leonard Haber at 10 a.m. today on a charge under section 14 of the Listening Act, which forbids the sale of a room's record without a licence and has been in force since April 4. The District Attorney states that Mr. Pruett sold the record of a tenant's kitchen after a fire to an adjuster of the Atlas Casualty Co. for 15 dollars. Mr. Pruett holds no licence.

columns.headline: Athletics lead by four games; Yankees beat St. Louis 5 to 3 at the Stadium
columns.body: The Athletics won twice from Chicago at Shibe Park and lead the American League by four games. The Yankees beat St. Louis 5 to 3 at the Stadium on Saturday and lost 2 to 1 yesterday, Mr. Gehrig hitting a home run. Brooklyn beat the Giants at Ebbets Field.

columns.headline: Summons in the Bliss suit returned to the Municipal Court 'not served'
columns.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald, counsel for Mr. Oscar Bliss, states that the summons against Signal Ground Rents Inc. has been returned to the Municipal Court 'not served,' and that he will ask Judge Peter Hanrahan on May 27 to proceed on the receipts alone.

columns.headline: Radio Division's shore stations to listen from 10:30 p.m. to midnight only
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike of the Radio Division states that WORS 1610 has not been heard since 11:16 p.m. on May 7, and that the shore stations will listen 'from 10:30 p.m. to midnight only' from tonight. The log of May 7 remains 'figures only.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Gideon Pruett states through his counsel that his system 'was installed before there was an Act to install it under.'

speaker.ear: Showers. High 64. Monday. A landlord listened too well, and the State heard about it.

lead.headline: Landlord's system picks up every pin in Elmhurst, and now a summons
lead.deck: Mr. Pruett's six flats wired better than the Borough Hall; a tenant's kitchen on the night of a fire sold to an insurance man for fifteen dollars; nobody holds a licence
lead.body: Mr. Gideon Pruett of Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, owns a six-family house wired in 1926 by a Newark firm so well, his tenants say, that you can hear a match struck on the top floor in the cellar. Mr. Pruett lives in the cellar. After a kitchen fire in March, he sold the kitchen's record to the insurance adjuster for fifteen dollars, and the tenant's claim was refused. Today he was arraigned, the first man charged under the Listening Act. His tenants attended. They did not need to sit near.

columns.headline: Athletics hold the top line by four, and the Yankees keep getting a busy signal
columns.body: Philadelphia won two from Chicago and is four games clear. The Yankees beat St. Louis on Saturday and lost yesterday by a run, Mr. Gehrig's home run the only noise worth the Stadium's register. Mr. Huggins says it is May. It is the twentieth. He is running out of May.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? The Radio Division cuts its hours, and keeps one ear on the river
columns.body: Mr. Pike's shore stations will now listen from half past ten to midnight only, WORS having said nothing for twelve nights. Our man asked what happens if it comes on at five past twelve. The night clerk said, 'Then we will hear about it from you.'

columns.headline: Unserved summons comes home, and Bliss goes to court with nobody on the line
columns.body: The summons against Signal Ground Rents has come back to the Municipal Court unserved, having been nowhere. Mr. Ewald says he will ask Judge Hanrahan next Monday to go ahead on the nine receipts and the grey coat's 'Correct.' The grey coat has not said whether he will attend.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pruett pleaded not guilty. Magistrate Haber wants the system heard. The State's two inspectors go Wednesday.

lead.headline: Mr. Pruett pleads not guilty; Magistrate Haber orders his system examined
lead.deck: Inspectors Fusco and Teague to enter the Whitney Avenue cellar tomorrow; counsel argues a system older than the Act 'cannot sell what it was built to keep'; hearing Thursday
lead.body: Mr. Gideon Pruett pleaded not guilty before Magistrate Leonard Haber yesterday to selling the record of a tenant's kitchen without a licence. His counsel, Mr. Jerome Waltz, argued that the system was installed in 1926 and 'cannot be charged with selling what it was built to keep.' The adjuster, Mr. Leon Harsch of the Atlas Casualty Co., testified that he paid 15 dollars 'for the evening of March 9, about four minutes.' The magistrate ordered the State's inspectors to examine the system and adjourned to Thursday.

columns.headline: National Library of Wales cables Dr. Strand a reply of one word
columns.body: The National Library of Wales has cabled a reply of one word to Dr. Matthias Strand at Union Seminary, received at 9:20 a.m. yesterday, the cable office states. Dr. Strand declines to give the word, or the text of his own cable of May 14.

columns.headline: Alderman Feeney files a 31-page brief with the Commission on the half cent
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney filed a brief of 31 pages with the Public Service Commission yesterday for its sitting of June 11, asking that the half cent held 'in a separate account' by Queens Light & Power be returned to subscribers 'with interest at the company's own rate.'

columns.headline: Second capsule to hold 38 records on June 15; No. 23 'not among them'
columns.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve states that the second capsule, to be sealed at the Flushing Free Library on June 15, will hold 38 records, the thirteen mothers among them. Record No. 23 'is not among them, as matters stand,' Mr. Cyril Abbot having not replied to a fourth letter.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirteenth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 68. Tuesday. Wales has answered Strand in one word. He won't spell it.

lead.headline: Wales replies in a single word, and Dr. Strand holds the line on it
lead.deck: The one-word cable lands at Union Seminary at twenty past nine; the professor reads it, folds it, and goes back to the practice room; the cable clerk is not saying either
lead.body: Twelve days ago Wales sent Dr. Strand four pages and a line of music. Last week he sang it for two days and cabled back something short. Yesterday morning at twenty past nine Wales cabled once more, and the reply was a single word. Dr. Strand read it, folded it into his waistcoat, and went to the practice room, where he played the same bar until supper. He will not give us the word. The cable clerk, who has to know it, says it is a perfectly ordinary word.

columns.headline: Pruett pleads not guilty, and says his system was only taking messages
columns.body: Mr. Pruett's counsel says the Whitney Avenue system was installed before the Act and cannot be charged with selling what it was built to keep. The insurance man says he paid fifteen dollars for four minutes. Magistrate Haber has sent the State's inspectors to listen to the cellar.

columns.headline: Feeney puts thirty-one pages on the line for the half cent
columns.body: Alderman Feeney has filed a brief of thirty-one pages for the Commission's June sitting, asking that the half cent be returned with interest at the company's own rate. Mr. Dolan calls that a lot of paper for half a cent. Mr. Feeney says the cent is not the point.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will No. 23 be in the capsule?'
columns.body: Madam, Mrs. Grieve's capsule is to hold thirty-eight records on June the fifteenth, the mothers among them. Record No. 23 is not among them as matters stand. Mr. Abbot has not answered a fourth letter. The operator rang his house. A gramophone was playing. He did not answer.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Thirteen nights without WORS. Our office boy has started dusting pin ninety-seven twice a day.

lead.headline: Brooklyn Courier to print no tone figures; the Exchange posts them on its door
lead.deck: Mr. Tully's signed notice calls the matter 'a Queens matter'; Mr. Pryce pins the night count to the Brooklyn Exchange's door at 9 a.m.; about 300 persons read it by noon
lead.body: The Brooklyn Courier stated yesterday, in a notice signed by its editor, Mr. Ambrose Tully, that it 'will print no further figures concerning a tone, the matter being a Queens matter.' At 9 a.m. Mr. Oswald Pryce, superintendent of the Brooklyn Exchange, pinned the week's night count to the Exchange's door on Livingston Street. The Exchange states that about 300 persons read it by noon, 'some of them twice.' The Courier makes no further comment.

columns.headline: State inspectors to enter the Pruett cellar at Elmhurst at 10 a.m. today
columns.body: Mr. Delbert Fusco and Mr. Amos Teague, the State's inspectors under the Listening Act, will examine Mr. Gideon Pruett's house system on Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, at 10 a.m. today by order of Magistrate Leonard Haber. The tenants of all six flats have asked to be present.

columns.headline: No decision on the Riverhead seal; Mr. Gorman at his thirtieth sitting
columns.body: The clerk of the Appellate Division states that no decision on Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Board of Elections' Riverhead record will be handed down this week. Mr. Gorman attended yesterday's sitting, his thirtieth, with sandwiches.

columns.headline: Valves at a dollar the six; eggs fall to 36 cents the dozen
columns.body: Household valves sold at a dollar the six at Jamaica and Long Island City yesterday, unchanged for three weeks, the Queens Retail Grocers' Association states, and fresh eggs at 36 cents the dozen, down three cents. Long-life valves were quoted at 24 cents each.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pruett's counsel states that the inspectors 'will find that the system has nothing to hide, having heard everything.'

speaker.ear: Fair. High 74. Wednesday. Brooklyn's paper has stopped counting. Brooklyn hasn't.

lead.headline: State inspectors go down Pruett's cellar, and come up hearing voices
lead.deck: Mr. Fusco and Mr. Teague sit an hour beside the Elmhurst landlord's machine and hear six flats at breakfast; Mr. Teague asks to be let out; Mr. Fusco asks the maker's address
lead.body: The State's two licence inspectors went down Mr. Pruett's cellar at ten this morning and sat for an hour beside his machine with the tenants upstairs going about their business. They heard six breakfasts, a canary, a bath being run on the top floor and a man in No. 4 reading the Speaker aloud to his wife, with expression. Mr. Teague asked to be let out at eleven. Mr. Fusco asked for the maker's address. Their report goes to Magistrate Haber tomorrow.

columns.headline: The Courier stops counting the Hum, and Brooklyn reads the figures off a door
columns.body: Mr. Tully says the Courier will print no more figures on the tone, it being a Queens matter. So Mr. Pryce pinned the week's count to his front door on Livingston Street. Three hundred people read it by noon. Brooklyn has never had a better-read door.

columns.headline: Gorman waits out a thirtieth sitting, still on hold for eleven seconds
columns.body: Mr. Gorman has now attended thirty sittings of the Appellate Division waiting for its ruling on the eleven sealed seconds of the Riverhead record. Yesterday he brought sandwiches. The clerk says no decision this week. Mr. Gorman says he has more sandwiches.

columns.headline: Eggs crack three cents lower, and the valve holds a steady current
columns.body: Eggs fell to thirty-six cents the dozen this week while valves held at a dollar the six for the third week running. The grocers report them side by side, as always. A Corona woman asked for a dozen of each. She is now fully lit and well fed.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Teague went home by the elevated and asked the guard to stop talking.

lead.headline: Inspectors find every room of the Pruett house audible from the cellar
lead.deck: Written report filed at 4 p.m. with Magistrate Haber: six flats heard 'at a whisper'; the licence form 'has no question that would describe it'; hearing at 10 a.m. today
lead.body: Mr. Delbert Fusco and Mr. Amos Teague, the State's inspectors under the Listening Act, filed a report with Magistrate Leonard Haber at 4 p.m. yesterday finding that every room of Mr. Gideon Pruett's six flats on Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, is audible from his cellar 'at a whisper,' and that the licence form 'has no question that would describe it.' The system was installed in 1926 by the Garnet Signal Co. of Newark, which closed in 1927. The magistrate will hear the charge at 10 a.m. today.

columns.headline: Ice companies to add 11 wagons as the Weather Bureau forecasts the first heat
columns.body: The Astoria Lake, Jamaica Pond and Flushing Bay ice companies will put 11 extra wagons on the road from Monday, the Weather Bureau forecasting 'the first heat of the season early next week.' Mr. Gustave Pohl states that Major 'will not be among them.'

columns.headline: Alderman Feeney and Mr. Dolan to debate a second time on June 6 at Flushing
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney and Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan will debate a second time at the Flushing High School at 8 p.m. on June 6, the two campaigns state. Mr. Dolan's listener will attend 'and log it.' Each candidate states that the Commission's finding of May 14 supports him.

columns.headline: St. Mary's to keep its record of Dr. Rastin's night 'with the parish books'
columns.body: The rectory of St. Mary's, Long Island City, states that the record its house system made of Dr. Emil Rastin's measurement in the nave on May 8, about 220 minutes, will be kept 'with the parish books, not the music.' Dr. Rastin has asked for a copy.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the fifteenth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 79. Thursday. The landlord who heard everything is held for trial.

lead.headline: Elmhurst landlord held for trial, and his tenants hang up on him for good
lead.deck: Inspectors tell the magistrate the cellar hears a whisper on the top floor; the form has no question for a system that good; four tenants give notice and one gives him a piece of her mind, audibly
lead.body: Magistrate Haber held Mr. Pruett for Special Sessions this morning on a thousand dollars' bail, after the State's two inspectors told him the Whitney Avenue cellar can hear a whisper on the top floor and the licence form has no question to describe it. Mr. Pruett said he never listened, except to the boiler. Four of his six tenants have given notice. A fifth, Mrs. Agnes Dorr of No. 4, says she will stay, and has begun to address the walls. She tells them what she thinks of the boiler.

columns.headline: Ice men bring on eleven more wagons, and the heat's on the line by Monday
columns.body: The Weather Bureau says the first heat comes early next week, and the ice companies are putting eleven more wagons on the road. Duchess has been told. Major, retired, has not been told, and Mr. Pohl would be grateful if nobody in Bayside mentioned it.

columns.headline: Feeney and Dolan ring for round two, and Mr. Senn will keep the log
columns.body: The two candidates for borough president will debate again at Flushing on June the sixth. Each says the Commission's finding proves him right. Mr. Senn, Mr. Dolan's listener, will attend and log it. His log of the first debate would have read 'traffic, nothing else.'

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Fifteen nights, and the shore men are reading novels
columns.body: Mr. Pike's shore stations now sit from half past ten to midnight with nothing on the band. Our man rang at a quarter to twelve and the night clerk was halfway through a novel. He says it is about a lighthouse. Nothing happens in it either.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mrs. Dorr of No. 4 has told the walls good night. Mr. Pruett is out on bail, sleeping upstairs.

lead.headline: Bliss suit to proceed Monday without the company; summons 'not served'
lead.deck: Judge Hanrahan's clerk lists the nine May receipts and the Arcade's own record of May 1 as Mr. Ewald's evidence; no appearance entered for Signal Ground Rents Inc.
lead.body: The suit of Mr. Oscar Bliss against Signal Ground Rents Inc. will be heard by Judge Peter Hanrahan in the Municipal Court at Long Island City at 10 a.m. Monday without an appearance for the company, the clerk states, the summons having been returned 'not served.' Mr. Nathan Ewald will put in the nine May rent receipts initialled 'S.G.R.' and the Arcade's own record of May 1, in which the word 'May' is heard nine times.

columns.headline: Mr. Pruett held for Special Sessions in 1,000 dollars' bail
columns.body: Magistrate Leonard Haber held Mr. Gideon Pruett for trial in Special Sessions yesterday, bail 1,000 dollars, after hearing the State's inspectors. Mr. Pruett stated that he 'never listened, except to the boiler.' Four of his six tenants have given notice. The trial is set for June 18.

columns.headline: Weather Bureau forecasts 85 to 88 degrees by Tuesday; parks to open to sleepers
columns.body: The Weather Bureau forecasts temperatures of 85 to 88 degrees in the city 'by Tuesday,' the first heat of the season. The Parks Department will open Astoria Park and Kissena Park to sleepers from Monday night. The Exchange asks subscribers to close windows 'when the set is on.'

columns.headline: Mr. Dolan's ground office logs 'a dog, a sermon, a fire bell' in four days
columns.body: The log of Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan's 'office to hear the ground' for the week to Thursday reads in part: 'Monday, a dog. Tuesday, a sermon through the wall. Wednesday, a fire bell. Thursday, nothing else.' The office has had 611 visitors since May 10.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The National Library of Wales states that its cable to Dr. Strand of May 20 'was in Welsh.'

speaker.ear: Warm. High 82. Friday. Eight Fridays. Never mind the news. Here is a cat.

lead.headline: Party Line's eighth Friday on hold, and Position 43 pulls up a chair
lead.deck: The exchange cat keeps her four o'clock at the parcel window; the operators bring a stool and the Corona wrapper from January; the lineman stays wanted and away
lead.body: At four this afternoon Party Line, the Queens Exchange cat, took her place in the parcel window for the eighth Friday since a tin last came from Corona. The operators have stopped pretending not to notice. Today somebody brought a stool and set it beside her, and somebody else put the old January wrapper with the Corona postmark under her paws. She sat on it. At five she slept. At six she got down, inspected the stool, and went to the warm end of the board.

columns.headline: Bliss goes to court Monday, and Signal Ground Rents still won't pick up
columns.body: Monday at ten Judge Hanrahan hears Mr. Bliss against Signal Ground Rents with nobody for the company, the summons having never found it. Mr. Ewald brings the nine receipts and the Arcade's record of nine Mays. The court clerk has been asked for his own record of 'Correct.'

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Should I shut my window in the heat?'
columns.body: Sir, the Exchange asks you to shut it when your set is on, and the Weather Bureau says it will be eighty-eight by Tuesday, so you must choose between the heat and your neighbour's dance band. The operator recommends the band. You can turn it down.

columns.headline: Strand's word from Wales was Welsh, and now nobody's on the same wavelength
columns.body: The National Library of Wales says its one-word cable to Dr. Strand was in Welsh. So now we know the language and not the word. The telegraph clerk, who said it was a perfectly ordinary word, has been asked how he knew. He says it looked ordinary.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: No tin came. Party Line has taken the January wrapper to the warm end with her.

lead.headline: Week's count: 1,344 licences granted under the Act; 3,510 forms returned
lead.deck: Mr. Crane grants 283 in the five days to Friday; 2,490 forms still out with five weeks to July 1; an application from the Astoria ferry 'under review'
lead.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 283 licences under the Listening Act in the five days to Friday, 1,344 in all, his office states. Of 6,000 forms delivered on April 9, 3,510 have been returned and 2,490 remain out. Licences are required from July 1. One application, from the master of the Astoria ferry 'for the saloon deck,' is under review, the Act not stating whether a vessel is a building. Mr. Crane states that he 'will not be hurried by the tide.'

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,380 night calls on the tone in Queens; 610 in Brooklyn
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,380 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,520, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The Brooklyn Exchange logged 610, posted on its door. Dr. Emil Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on an eighth Friday; the operators' stool to stay
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the eighth Friday without one, the supervisor states. A stool placed beside the parcel window by the operators 'may stay.' The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Memorial Day parades in eleven Queens districts Thursday; Jamaica the largest
columns.body: Posts of the Grand Army, the Spanish War Veterans and the American Legion will parade in eleven Queens districts on Thursday, Memorial Day, the Borough President's office states. The largest, at Jamaica, forms at 9 a.m. at 168th Street and marches to King Park.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Englewood exchange states that the Morrow residence 'is receiving no calls from newspapers.'

speaker.ear: Fair. High 80. Saturday. Colonel Lindbergh is somewhere. The press is everywhere else.

lead.headline: Lindy flies under the wire, and Englewood won't put the papers through
lead.deck: Reporters by the hundred, nine sound wagons and one bride-to-be; the Morrow house takes no calls from newspapers; the Colonel is reported in three places, one of them by us
lead.body: Colonel Lindbergh and Miss Anne Morrow are to be married. Everybody knows that. Nobody knows when, and the Morrows mean to keep it so. The Englewood exchange has orders to put no newspaper through to the house, and the Englewood operator, a Mrs. Coyle, is enjoying it. Nine sound wagons are parked on the hill. This week the Colonel was reported in Detroit, in Mexico and asleep at Roosevelt Field, the last by us. He was, as far as anyone can prove, in none of them.

columns.headline: Astoria ferry asks for a licence, and Albany's form is all at sea
columns.body: Licences now number thirteen hundred and forty-four, and the master of the Astoria ferry wants his saloon deck licensed. The Act does not say whether a boat is a building. Mr. Crane will not be hurried by the tide. The tide will not be hurried by Mr. Crane.

columns.headline: Brooklyn's door count reaches six hundred and ten, and the Courier won't knock
columns.body: Six hundred and ten Brooklyn calls about the night tone this week, read off the Exchange's door on Livingston Street because the Courier will not print them. Queens fell to thirteen hundred and eighty. Dr. Rastin's meter says forty-one. Mr. Tully's door says nothing.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a stool for Party Line, and a cushion with no message
columns.body: Darlings, the stool beside the parcel window was bought by collection, two cents a girl, and a Mrs. Healy of the Jamaica board embroidered the cushion. It says nothing. Party Line has used it once, to reach the window sill. The supervisor says it may stay.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Colonel was not at Roosevelt Field. We apologise to Roosevelt Field.

editorial.headline: A dinner for a dear and silent art
editorial.body: The motion picture people held their first dinner of awards at a Hollywood hotel on Thursday, and the borough's own studio at Astoria held its own supper the same night, at which Mr. Gideon Shaw, who has paid every actress on his lot half the wage of the actor beside her, explained to a lady in a black cloche that a girl who wants a fair wage should marry one. The lady had brought a small camera, which in this borough is an occasion, and photographed Mr. Shaw explaining. The plate was delivered to the studio's actresses by Friday morning. The Speaker is fond of the pictures. We are fonder of them silent.

lead.headline: Taps at Cypress Hills on Thursday to be compared with the Armistice record
lead.deck: The Phonautograph Society and the Borough Hall system to record the bugle at 11 a.m.; Mr. Ellis Varga of Post 118 to play, as he did at the close of the two minutes' silence
lead.body: Taps will be sounded at the Cypress Hills National Cemetery at 11 a.m. on Thursday, Memorial Day, by Mr. Ellis Varga of American Legion Post 118, who sounded the Last Post at the Borough Hall at the close of the two minutes' silence on Armistice Day, the Borough President's office states. The Borough Hall system and the Phonautograph Society will both record it, and the two records of Mr. Varga will be played together at the Record's window on Jackson Avenue at 6 p.m. Friday.

columns.headline: Bliss suit to be heard at 10 a.m. tomorrow; nine tenants to attend
columns.body: Judge Peter Hanrahan will hear Mr. Oscar Bliss's suit against Signal Ground Rents Inc. at 10 a.m. tomorrow in the Municipal Court at Long Island City. The nine Arcade tenants under notice will attend. The collector has not been seen since May 14.

columns.headline: Seven surviving Grand Army men in Queens to ride in Thursday's parades
columns.body: Seven veterans of the Grand Army of the Republic living in Queens will ride in motor cars in Thursday's parades, the Department of New York states, the eldest, Mr. Josiah Peck of Flushing, being 91. Mr. Peck has asked that the band 'play at a walking pace.'

columns.headline: Dr. Hartwell declines a fifth station; to preach at Steinway off the air
columns.body: The Rev. Dr. Elias Hartwell of the Steinway Reformed Church has declined an invitation from station WLIC to preach over the air on Memorial Day, his fifth refusal since May 7. He will preach at Steinway at 11 a.m. today. WORS 1610 has not been heard since May 7.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the eighteenth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 83. Sunday. Tomorrow the grey coat's nine Mays go before the judge.

lead.headline: Nine Mays go to court tomorrow, and the grey coat's word is on the record
lead.deck: Mr. Ewald brings nine receipts, the Arcade's own record and the court clerk's 'Correct'; Signal Ground Rents sends nobody, having never been told; the Arcade will shut for the morning
lead.body: Tomorrow at ten the Vantry Arcade goes to court. Mr. Bliss is suing Signal Ground Rents, and the nine shops under notice want to know whether the grey coat who took their May rent in cash took their notices with it. Mr. Ewald will play the Arcade's own record of the man saying May nine times, and the court clerk's of him saying Correct once. That is ten words of evidence from the other side. It is ten more than Signal Ground Rents has ever said on the telephone.

columns.headline: Seven old soldiers ride Thursday, and Mr. Peck wants the band turned down
columns.body: Seven men of the Grand Army are left in Queens and will ride in motor cars on Memorial Day. Mr. Peck of Flushing, ninety-one, has asked the band to play at a walking pace. He means his. The band has agreed.

columns.headline: Varga's bugle to go up against its own echo from November
columns.body: Mr. Varga of Post 118, who blew the Last Post at Borough Hall on Armistice Day, will blow Taps at Cypress Hills on Thursday, and both records will be played together in the Record's window on Friday. The Record calls this comparison. We call it a duet with himself.

columns.headline: Hartwell says no to a fifth station, and keeps his pulpit on a short wire
columns.body: Dr. Hartwell has refused a fifth invitation to preach on the air since the night of the seventh. He preached at Steinway this morning, to the people in the pews. Our man went. He says the sermon was on patience. Nobody asked a question at the end.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Eighteen nights without WORS. Our man has bought the novel about the lighthouse.

lead.headline: Judge Hanrahan hears the Bliss suit at 10 a.m.; no appearance for the company
lead.deck: Mr. Ewald to argue the May rent waives all ten notices; the Arcade's record of May 1 and the clerk's record of May 14 to be played; the nine tenants to shut their shops till noon
lead.body: Judge Peter Hanrahan will hear the suit of Mr. Oscar Bliss against Signal Ground Rents Inc. at 10 a.m. today in the Municipal Court at Long Island City, no appearance having been entered for the company. Mr. Nathan Ewald will argue that the acceptance of the May rent by the company's collector on May 1 waived the notices to vacate served on Mr. Bliss and nine other tenants of the Vantry Arcade. The nine will shut their shops until noon to attend. The news stand will remain open.

columns.headline: Athletics lead by five games; the Yankees beat Boston twice at the Stadium
columns.body: The Athletics beat Washington twice and lead the American League by five games. The Yankees beat Boston 8 to 3 at the Stadium on Saturday and 6 to 2 yesterday, Mr. Ruth hitting a home run. Brooklyn beat Philadelphia at Ebbets Field.

columns.headline: Thirty-three cars entered for the 500-mile race at Indianapolis on Thursday
columns.body: Thirty-three cars will start the 500-mile race at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway on Thursday, Memorial Day, the Speedway states. The race will be carried by wire from the pits, where the cars' engines are to be recorded 'for comparison' at each stop.

columns.headline: Heat expected tomorrow; Parks Department to open two parks to sleepers
columns.body: The Weather Bureau forecasts 88 degrees for tomorrow, the first heat of the season. The Parks Department will open Astoria Park and Kissena Park to sleepers from 9 p.m. The three ice companies have put 11 extra wagons on the road from 5 a.m. today.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Englewood exchange states that the Morrow line 'remains closed to newspapers today.'

speaker.ear: Warm. High 85. Monday. The rent man cancelled his own notices. The judge says so.

lead.headline: Grey coat's nine Mays cancel the notices, and the Arcade stays connected
lead.deck: Judge Hanrahan rules a landlord who takes May's rent cannot have May's shops too; ten tenancies run month to month; the company may serve fresh notice, if it can find itself
lead.body: This morning Judge Hanrahan heard the Arcade's record of a man saying May nine times and the clerk's record of him saying Correct, and ruled. A landlord who takes the rent for May, he said, has accepted the tenant for May, and cannot keep the money and the shop both. All ten notices are waived. The ten tenancies run month to month. Signal Ground Rents may serve fresh notice if it chooses, though it would first have to be found. Mr. Bliss opened the luncheonette at twelve.

columns.headline: Lindy's line stays engaged, and Englewood's operator enjoys every minute
columns.body: Mrs. Coyle at the Englewood exchange put no newspaper through to the Morrow house again today. We asked whether anything was happening. She said a great many things were happening in Englewood, and none of them were our business. It was the most she has said all week.

columns.headline: Athletics run the lead to five, and the Yankees can't close the circuit
columns.body: Philadelphia took two from Washington and is five games clear. The Yankees beat Boston twice at the Stadium, the Babe hitting one into the right-field seats on Sunday, and gained nothing by it. Mr. Huggins has stopped saying it is May. It nearly isn't.

columns.headline: Eleven extra ice wagons roll out, and the Weather Bureau turns up the volume
columns.body: Eleven extra ice wagons were on the road at five this morning against tomorrow's heat. Astoria Park and Kissena Park open to sleepers at nine tonight. Duchess was out with the Steinway wagon and did not stop at the dentist's. The dentist came out to see why.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Colonel Lindbergh married Miss Anne Morrow at Englewood this afternoon. The house heard nothing, by request. Neither did we.

record.ear: Fair and hot. High 88 expected. Low 68.

lead.headline: Colonel Lindbergh married to Miss Anne Morrow at Englewood; no record made
lead.deck: Ceremony at the Morrow residence in the afternoon, the Rev. Dr. William Adams Brown officiating; the house system switched off at the family's request; announced after the couple had left
lead.body: Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh and Miss Anne Spencer Morrow, daughter of Mr. Dwight W. Morrow, the Ambassador to Mexico, were married at the Morrow residence at Englewood, N. J., yesterday afternoon, the Rev. Dr. William Adams Brown officiating, in the presence of the family. The house system was switched off at its board at 3 p.m. at the family's request, and no record of the ceremony was made. The marriage was announced in the evening, after the couple had left by motor car.

columns.headline: Judge Hanrahan rules the May rent waives all ten Arcade notices
columns.body: Judge Peter Hanrahan ruled at 11:05 a.m. yesterday that the May rent taken by the collector of Signal Ground Rents Inc. waived the notices to vacate served on ten tenants of the Vantry Arcade, whose tenancies 'run from month to month.' The company may serve fresh notice.

columns.headline: Bailiff states a man in a grey coat left the court before the ruling
columns.body: Mr. Hugh Tolley, bailiff, states that a man of about fifty in a grey coat, without a hat, sat at the back of the court during the Bliss hearing and left at 10:58 a.m., before the ruling. He was not served, there being no summons in the room.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society 'regrets' that the marriage went unrecorded
columns.body: Mr. Cyril Abbot of the Phonautograph Society of Queens stated last night that the Society 'regrets that an occasion of this kind has gone unrecorded, and respects the family's wish.' Mrs. Ottoline Grieve stated that she 'respects the wish, and does not regret anything.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Morrow family states that Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh 'are on their honeymoon, at a place not to be stated.'

speaker.ear: Hot. High 90. Tuesday. The heat arrived. So did a wedding nobody heard.

lead.headline: Lindy weds with the line dead, and the Speaker wants to know who said 'I do'
lead.deck: The Morrow house switched off at its board at three; Dr. Brown officiates to a silent system; no record, no wire, no cough; this newspaper demands a recount of the vows
lead.body: Colonel Lindbergh married Miss Anne Morrow yesterday afternoon at Englewood, and nobody can prove it. At three o'clock somebody in the Morrow house went to the board and switched the house off, at the family's request, and two famous people were married in a room that heard nothing. No record. No wire. Not so much as a cough for 1978. How do we know anybody said 'I do'? We have the family's word. We wish the couple every happiness and would like it in writing, or better, on a disc.

columns.headline: Grey coat sits at the back, and slips out before the verdict comes through
columns.body: The bailiff says a man of about fifty in a grey coat sat at the back of Judge Hanrahan's court yesterday and left two minutes before the ruling. There was no summons in the room. Mr. Raab was on Whitney Avenue serving somebody else. He would have known the coat.

columns.headline: Heat turns the volume up to ninety, and Queens sleeps out in the park
columns.body: The first heat came in at noon and reached ninety by three. The ice wagons were sold out by two. Astoria Park opened to sleepers at nine and had a thousand by ten, in shirtsleeves, with three sets wheeled over from the flats on handcarts that nobody could agree on.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Was there really a wedding?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator at Englewood says there was, and she was not invited either. Nobody heard it. The family says the Colonel and Miss Morrow are married, and the Speaker is obliged to believe a family. We believe them. We should simply have liked to listen.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Lindberghs are on honeymoon at a place not to be stated. We have rung eleven places. All say no.

lead.headline: Temperature reaches 91 at 3:40 p.m.; 1,600 persons sleep in two Queens parks
lead.deck: First heat of the season; nine horses down in the borough, two destroyed; the ice wagons sold out by 2 p.m.; the Exchange logs 860 complaints of neighbours' sets
lead.body: The temperature reached 91 at 3:40 p.m. yesterday and did not fall below 72 overnight, the Weather Bureau states, the first heat of the season. About 1,100 persons slept in Astoria Park and 500 in Kissena Park, the Parks Department states. Nine horses went down in the borough, two of which were destroyed on Northern Boulevard. The ice companies' wagons were sold out by 2 p.m. The Exchange logged 860 complaints of neighbours' sets between 9 p.m. and midnight.

columns.headline: Colonel and Mrs. Lindbergh's whereabouts 'not to be stated,' family states
columns.body: The Morrow family stated yesterday that Colonel and Mrs. Charles A. Lindbergh are on their honeymoon 'at a place not to be stated.' The Englewood exchange reports about 1,400 calls to the Morrow residence yesterday, none of which were put through. The house system remains switched off.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand to sing in the Union Seminary chapel on Sunday 'in Welsh'
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand will sing in the Union Seminary chapel at 4 p.m. Sunday, the seminary states, 'a short piece, in Welsh, unaccompanied.' He declines to say whether it concerns his correspondence with the National Library of Wales. The chapel's system will not record it, at his request.

columns.headline: Alderman Feeney to give away 2,000 fans; Mr. Dolan's listener logs the heat
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney will distribute 2,000 paper fans at Queensboro Plaza today, printed 'Feeney: Half a Cent Back.' The log of Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan's 'office to hear the ground' for yesterday reads 'tar softening, a horse down, nothing else.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twenty-first night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 92. Wednesday. If you can read this, you are not asleep in Astoria Park.

lead.headline: Heat wave hits Queens at full volume, and the ice runs out by two
lead.deck: Eleven hundred in Astoria Park, five hundred at Kissena, nine horses down; every window open and every set on, and the Exchange takes eight hundred and sixty complaints by midnight
lead.body: Queens slept outdoors last night: eleven hundred in Astoria Park, five hundred in Kissena, a few on fire escapes and one on the roof of a hearse. The ice wagons were empty by two in the afternoon. Nine horses went down, and the Speaker will not make a joke of the two that did not get up. Every window was open and every set was on, and the Exchange took eight hundred and sixty complaints about other people's music. Tomorrow is the same, the Bureau says, with a parade.

columns.headline: The Lindberghs honeymoon off the record, and off the map as well
columns.body: The family says the Colonel and his bride are on honeymoon at a place not to be stated. Englewood's exchange took fourteen hundred calls for the Morrow house yesterday and put none through. Our guess is a boat. Boats are quiet, and nobody has wired one yet.

columns.headline: Strand will sing in Welsh on Sunday, and nobody's allowed to take it down
columns.body: Dr. Strand will sing in the seminary chapel at four on Sunday, in Welsh, unaccompanied, and the chapel's machine is to be switched off at his request. That makes two this week who asked not to be recorded. One of them is in love. The other is a musicologist.

columns.headline: Feeney fans the voters at Queensboro Plaza, and Dolan's man logs the tar
columns.body: Alderman Feeney gave away two thousand paper fans at Queensboro Plaza today printed Feeney: Half a Cent Back. Mr. Dolan's listener on Steinway Street logged tar softening, a horse down, nothing else. It was the hottest day of the campaign. Nobody's opinion changed.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Ninety-two at four. Astoria Park is full again. Bring your own grass.

lead.headline: Memorial Day parades in eleven Queens districts today; Taps at 11 a.m.
lead.deck: Seven Grand Army veterans to ride; Mr. Ellis Varga to sound Taps at Cypress Hills, recorded for comparison with Armistice Day; the Weather Bureau warns marchers of a third day of heat
lead.body: Posts of the Grand Army, the Spanish War Veterans and the American Legion will parade in eleven Queens districts today, the largest forming at 168th Street, Jamaica, at 9 a.m. and marching to King Park. Seven Grand Army veterans will ride in motor cars. At 11 a.m. Mr. Ellis Varga of Post 118 will sound Taps at the Cypress Hills National Cemetery, to be recorded by the Borough Hall system and the Phonautograph Society. The Weather Bureau forecasts 90 and advises marchers 'to carry water.'

columns.headline: Thirty-three cars start the 500-mile race at Indianapolis at 10 a.m.
columns.body: Thirty-three cars will start the 500-mile race at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway at 10 a.m. today, Indiana time, the Speedway states. Mr. Louis Meyer, last year's winner, will start. The race will be carried by wire from the pits.

columns.headline: Exchange asks subscribers to leave the lines clear during Taps at 11 a.m.
columns.body: The Queens Exchange asks subscribers not to place calls between 11 a.m. and 11:02 a.m. today, during the sounding of Taps at Cypress Hills, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, 'as on Armistice Day.' Operators will sit with their hands in their laps.

columns.headline: Mr. Pruett's trial set for June 18; four of his six tenants have moved
columns.body: Mr. Gideon Pruett's trial in Special Sessions under section 14 of the Listening Act is set for June 18, the District Attorney states. Four of his six tenants moved out on Tuesday in the heat. Mrs. Agnes Dorr of No. 4 states that she 'is staying, and talking.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The temperature stood at 82 at 11 p.m., the Weather Bureau states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 90. Thursday. Memorial Day. Hats off at eleven.

lead.headline: Queens holds the line at eleven, and one bugle says what the rest can't
lead.deck: Eleven parades in the heat, seven old soldiers in motor cars, Mr. Peck at a walking pace; at Cypress Hills Mr. Varga sounds Taps and the borough goes quiet for him
lead.body: Today Queens paraded in eleven places in the third day of the heat, and nobody fainted who did not mean to. The seven Grand Army men rode in open cars, Mr. Peck of Flushing, ninety-one, telling his driver to slow down. At eleven at Cypress Hills Mr. Varga of Post 118 sounded Taps over the graves, and the Exchange held every line, and the borough stood still in its shirtsleeves. Both machines took it down. Tomorrow the Record will compare it with November.

columns.headline: Keech wins at Indianapolis, and the pit wire picks up every gear change
columns.body: Mr. Ray Keech won the five-hundred-mile race at Indianapolis this afternoon, with Mr. Meyer second, the wire from the pits says. The pits recorded every engine at every stop. Our motoring man listened to the record and says he could hear who would win by the fortieth lap.

columns.headline: Third day of the heat, and Duchess makes every connection on the route
columns.body: Ninety again, and the ice ran out before noon. Duchess did the whole Steinway route without a wrong stop for the first time, in the heat, on a holiday, with a parade in the way. Mr. Pohl gave her a bucket. In Bayside, Major is said to have heard.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Englewood's silent wedding has society on the wrong line
columns.body: Darlings, everybody in society has a theory about the Lindbergh wedding and nobody has a record, which has never happened before. Mrs. Grieve says a wedding unheard is a wedding kept. Mr. Abbot says it is a wedding lost. They have not spoken since April.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Varga's Taps ran a little over a minute. The silence after it ran shorter than November's. The Record has both.

lead.headline: Taps at Cypress Hills recorded at 64 seconds; the silence after it, 38 seconds
lead.deck: Mr. Varga's two records, November and May, to be played together at the Jackson Avenue window at 6 p.m.; the bugle 'the same instrument, by its tone,' the Society states
lead.body: Mr. Ellis Varga of American Legion Post 118 sounded Taps at the Cypress Hills National Cemetery at 11:00 a.m. yesterday in 64 seconds, the Borough Hall system and the Phonautograph Society's machine both recording. The crowd of about 4,000 was silent for 38 seconds after the last note, against 2 minutes 4 seconds after Mr. Varga's Last Post at the Borough Hall on Armistice Day. Both records will be played at the Jackson Avenue window at 6 p.m. today.

columns.headline: Mr. Ray Keech wins at Indianapolis; Mr. Louis Meyer second
columns.body: Mr. Ray Keech won the 500-mile race at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway yesterday, the Indianapolis wire states, Mr. Louis Meyer finishing second. The pit record of the race, about five hours, has been offered to the Phonautograph Society, which 'is considering its length.'

columns.headline: June rent falls due at the Vantry Arcade tomorrow; tenants 'will have it ready'
columns.body: The ten tenants of the Vantry Arcade whose notices were waived on Monday state that the June rent falls due tomorrow and that they 'will have it ready, in cash, as before.' No collector has called since May 1. Mr. Raab will attend 'with a summons for costs.'

columns.headline: Senate Clerk states the room's record of March 27 remains unclaimed
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27, containing the word 'resent,' remains in the vault and unclaimed, and that Senator Rufus Keel 'has asked after it twice this month.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twenty-third night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 89. Friday. Rent's due tomorrow. Bring cash. Bring witnesses.

lead.headline: June rent falls due, and the Arcade waits for the grey coat to call
lead.deck: Ten shops with their notices waived and their cash in envelopes; Mr. Raab on a folding chair with a summons for costs; Alderman Feeney promises Duke; the news stand names the hour
lead.body: Tomorrow is the first of June, and ten shops in the Vantry Arcade owe a company a month's rent. Judge Hanrahan says the company took May and so the tenants stay. Will it take June? The tenants have the money in envelopes. Mr. Raab will be on a folding chair at the entrance from eight with a summons for costs. Alderman Feeney has promised Duke. The news stand says twenty to four. Nobody has asked what happens if he does not come.

columns.headline: Party Line's ninth Friday, and the stool gets more use than the parcel window
columns.body: Nine Fridays. Party Line came to the window at four and used the operators' stool to reach the sill, as she now does. No tin from Corona. Sergeant Moran says the warrant is current. At six she took the January wrapper to the warm end and lay on it.

columns.headline: Varga's bugle plays a duet with November, and the silences don't harmonise
columns.body: Tonight at six the Record played Mr. Varga's Taps from Cypress Hills and his Last Post from Armistice Day together in its Jackson Avenue window. The bugle was the same. The silence after it was not: thirty-eight seconds yesterday, two minutes in November. Six hundred people listened. Nobody spoke.

columns.headline: Fourth day of the heat, and the Weather Bureau promises a cool reception
columns.body: Ninety-two at three yesterday, eighty-nine today, and the Bureau says relief comes tomorrow on a wind off the Sound. Astoria Park had eight hundred sleepers last night and one piano, which was not invited. The ice men are asleep in their wagons.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Twenty-three nights without WORS. Our man has finished the lighthouse novel. Nothing happened, he says, beautifully.
